mainTopic: Does writing "I owe you" in a document, without a formal act of acquisition (קנין), create a real obligation? The גמרא keeps testing the view of ריש לקיש (no obligation) against the view of רבי יוחנן (yes, obligated).
overview: The גמרא continues the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about whether writing "I owe you" in a document creates a real debt without a קנין. First it pushes away a proof for רבי יוחנן. That case was about engagement agreements, which are binding by words alone, as רב גידל taught in the name of רב. Next it challenges ריש לקיש from a father who writes to a כהן, "I owe you five סלעים," for פדיון הבן. The answer is that the Torah already obligates the father, and the note only picks which כהן gets the money. The גמרא then asks why the son is not redeemed, and answers with עולא: by Torah law he is redeemed once the money is paid, but the חכמים decreed otherwise so people won't think one can redeem with documents. Finally רבא links the argument to one between רבי ישמעאל and בן ננס about a ערב who signs after the document was already signed. The גמרא begins to question that link, noting that according to בן ננס everyone agrees. That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The earlier case is about engagement agreements
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the earlier proof. That case was about a שטר פסיקתא, an engagement agreement, which follows the rule of רב גידל.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, that case is about engagement-agreement documents, and it follows רב גידל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof that was just brought for רבי יוחנן. It says the case there was a special kind of document: an engagement agreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier source seemed to show that a written promise is binding even without a קנין. The גמרא answers that this source is about money promised when a couple gets engaged. That kind of promise is binding for a special reason, so it proves nothing about an ordinary "I owe you" document.

keyTerms.meaning: Documents that record how much money each family promised when arranging a marriage
No. This is how the גמרא opens a rejection of a proof
And this follows the opinion of רב גידל

phrases.english: No, it is about documents of stipulation,
phrases.notes: These are papers listing what each set of parents promised to give the couple when the שידוך was arranged.

phrases.english: and it follows רב גידל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof for רבי יוחנן brought just before this section by explaining it as a special case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not say anything about which opinion is right.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The source is about engagement promises. Those are binding by words alone, so they cannot teach us about a regular written debt.

steps.title: רב גידל: engagement promises are binding by words alone
steps.stepSummary: רב גידל quotes רב. When two families agree on amounts for their children and the couple then becomes engaged, the promises become binding through words alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב גידל said in the name of רב: One side asks, "How much are you giving your son?" The answer is, "Such and such." The other asks, "How much are you giving your daughter?" The answer is, "Such and such." If the couple then went ahead with the קידושין, the promises are acquired. These are the things that are acquired just by saying them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the teaching of רב גידל that it just mentioned. Promises made between families when arranging a marriage become binding as soon as the couple does קידושין, with no קנין needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, a promise to give money needs a formal act (קנין) before it becomes binding. Here, words alone are enough, because the families made these promises so that the marriage would happen. Once the קידושין takes place, each family has gotten what it wanted. This explains why the document in the earlier case was binding without saying anything about ordinary debts.

keyTerms.meaning: Such and such, meaning a certain amount
They went ahead and did the קידושין
They acquired it, so it is now binding
Things that are acquired by words alone

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this teaching means every promise is binding without a קנין. It is a special rule only for money promised in arranging a marriage.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב גידל's rule is a well-known exception in the laws of acquisition, and it is used in halacha for engagement agreements.

phrases.english: As רב גידל said that רב said:
How much are you giving your son?
phrases.notes: This is the bride's family asking the groom's family.

phrases.english: Such and such.
And how much are you giving your daughter?
Such and such.
If they went ahead and did the betrothal, they acquired it.
These are the things
that are acquired by speech alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the teaching of רב גידל that step 1 relied on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money that families promise each other when arranging a marriage becomes binding by words alone, once the קידושין is done.

steps.title: New challenge: a written promise to a כהן for פדיון הבן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a source about a father who writes to a כהן, "I owe you five סלעים." He must pay, which seems to show that writing creates an obligation. That goes against ריש לקיש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If he wrote to a כהן, "I owe you five סלעים," he must give him five סלעים, and his son is not redeemed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to challenge ריש לקיש. A father wrote a note to a כהן promising five סלעים for redeeming his firstborn, and the halacha is that he must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father must pay because of what he wrote, even with no קנין. That sounds like רבי יוחנן, who holds that writing "I owe you" creates a debt. The source also rules that his son is not redeemed, even after the father pays. Steps 7-8 explain why.

keyTerms.meaning: Silver coins. Five of them are paid to a כהן for פדיון הבן
Redeemed. Used here for a firstborn son
A descendant of אהרן, who receives the redemption money

steps.confusionAlert: There are two separate rulings here. He owes the money, but the son is not redeemed, even after he pays. Steps 7 and 8 explain why.

phrases.english: Come and hear: If he wrote to a priest:
phrases.notes: This is a father arranging פדיון הבן for his firstborn son.

phrases.english: "That I owe you five sela",
he is obligated to give him five sela,
and his son is not redeemed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier proof was pushed away, the גמרא tries a new source against ריש לקיש.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that writing "I owe you" does not create an obligation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The father must pay just because he wrote the note, which shows that a written promise creates a binding debt.

steps.title: There the father already owes the money from the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this case is different. The father already owes five סלעים from the Torah, so the note is not what makes him owe.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because he is already bound to him by Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends ריש לקיש. In the פדיון הבן case, the father would owe the money even without writing anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah itself obligates every father of a firstborn to pay five סלעים. So the debt does not come from the written note, and the case cannot prove that writing creates an obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there
Bound or obligated
From the Torah

phrases.english: It is different there,
because he is obligated to him by Torah law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3 for ריש לקיש.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the obligation there has a different source.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the note itself made the father owe five סלעים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah already made him owe it. The note adds no new obligation, so ריש לקיש is not disproven.

steps.title: Then why did he write a note at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if he already owes the money from the Torah, what was the point of writing the note?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why did he write?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave. If the Torah already obligates him, writing seems pointless. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A document is usually written to create or prove an obligation. If the Torah already made him owe the money, the note seems to have no purpose. So the answer in step 4 needs some explaining.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Why?

phrases.english: If so, why did he write?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the father already owes the money from the Torah.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the debt already exists, writing a note serves no purpose. So why would the father bother?

steps.title: He wrote it to choose a particular כהן
steps.stepSummary: The note was written to pick one specific כהן to receive the redemption money.
steps.simpleTranslation: In order to choose a particular כהן for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the note was written: the father wanted to set aside one particular כהן for his son's פדיון. This defends ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the Torah, the father may give the five סלעים to any כהן he wants. The note did not create the debt. It only decided which כהן would get it. So the case still does not show that writing "I owe you" creates an obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: To pick out or choose

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs against ריש לקיש are pushed away. The engagement document is binding because of רב גידל's special rule, and the פדיון הבן note is binding because the Torah already obligates the father. The note only picks which כהן gets the money.

phrases.english: In order to select a priest for himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5, which keeps the answer of step 4 standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the document a different purpose: it picks a כהן rather than creating a debt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The note seemed pointless, which made the answer of step 4 look weak.
steps.terutzMaskana: The note picks which כהן gets the Torah-required money, so the answer stands and ריש לקיש is not disproven.

steps.title: Then why isn't the son redeemed?
steps.stepSummary: If the father truly owes the money from the Torah and the note only picked the כהן, why does the teaching say his son is not redeemed?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is his son not redeemed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last answer. If the note only picked which כהן gets the money, the son should be redeemed once the father pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said the father's debt comes from the Torah and the note only named the כהן. If that is true, nothing is wrong with this פדיון הבן, so the son should be redeemed. But the source said 'his son is not redeemed,' so the גמרא wants to know why.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is true
Why?
Redeemed (a בכור who has gone through פדיון הבן)

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: He means: if the note only picked which כהן gets the money, like Step 6 said.

phrases.english: why is his son not redeemed?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, בְּנוֹ אַמַּאי אֵינוֹ פָּדוּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 6 using another detail of the same source
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the father's debt is from the Torah and the note only picks a כהן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the debt is a real Torah debt and the כהן has been chosen, the son should be redeemed. Yet the source says he is not.

steps.title: עולא: a rabbinic decree about documents
steps.stepSummary: By Torah law the son is redeemed once the money is given. The חכמים said he is not redeemed so people won't think you can redeem with a document.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like עולא, who said: by Torah law he is redeemed once the father gives the money. So why did they say his son is not redeemed? It is a decree, so that people won't say one may redeem with documents.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a teaching of עולא. Under Torah law the son is fine. The 'not redeemed' rule is only a rabbinic גזירה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 asked why the son isn't redeemed if the debt is real. עולא splits the answer into two levels: Torah law says paying the money redeems him, and the חכמים added the 'not redeemed' rule. They worried people would think a שטר by itself can work as payment for פדיון הבן, when the Torah wants real money.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law (as opposed to a rabbinic rule)
When he gives (the money)
A protective decree of the חכמים
Documents, written notes

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'his son is not redeemed' as Torah law. עולא says that by Torah law the son is redeemed when the money is given. The 'not redeemed' rule is only a rabbinic safeguard.

phrases.english: It is in line with עולא.
For עולא said:
By Torah law, he is redeemed when he gives the money,
and what is the reason they said
'his son is not redeemed'?
It is a decree, lest people say
that one may redeem with documents.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits Torah law from a rabbinic decree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The source's 'not redeemed' shows the son stays unredeemed even by Torah law
steps.terutzMaskana: By Torah law he is redeemed once the money is given. The 'not redeemed' rule is a rabbinic גזירה against redeeming with documents.
steps.whatToRemember: The father's note to the כהן does not prove that writing creates a debt. The debt comes from the Torah. The son's 'not redeemed' status is only a rabbinic גזירה.

steps.title: רבא: this is an older argument of תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the argument matches an older one about a ערב who signs after the loan document was already signed. The first opinion says the lender collects from the ערב's free property.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: this is like an argument of תנאים. A ערב who appears after the signatures on documents: the lender collects from free property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new line. He links the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש to an older argument among תנאים. This step sets up the case, and the next step shows the two sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here a ערב signs on only after the loan document was already signed. The first ruling is that his promise does count. But it counts only like a spoken debt, so the lender can collect only from property the ערב still owns (נכסים בני חורין).

keyTerms.meaning: It is like an argument of the תנאים
Guarantor; someone who promises to pay if the borrower doesn't
The signing (of the witnesses)
Free property: property the person still owns and has not sold

phrases.english: רבא said: it is like an argument of תנאים:
A guarantor who appears after the signatures on documents,
the lender collects from free property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the back-and-forth ends, רבא shows the argument between the אמוראים has older roots in an argument of תנאים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A guarantee written after the document was signed lets the lender collect only from the ערב's free property.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל and בן ננס argue
steps.stepSummary: A real case came to רבי ישמעאל, and he said the lender collects from free property. בן ננס said the lender collects nothing at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: A case came before רבי ישמעאל, and he said: he collects from free property. בן ננס said to him: he does not collect, not from free property and not from sold property.
steps.whatsHappening: Now we see the actual argument between the תנאים. רבי ישמעאל says the late ערב must pay, and בן ננס says he owes nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל treats the late ערב's words as a real debt, even if a weaker one. בן ננס says those words create no debt at all. So the lender cannot collect from property the ערב still has, and not from property he sold.

keyTerms.meaning: A real case that happened
Property that was sold but carries a lien from the debt

phrases.english: A case came before רבי ישמעאל,
and he said: he collects from free property.
בן ננס said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ גּוֹבֶה לֹא מִנְּכָסִים בְּנֵי חוֹרִין
phrases.english: He does not collect, not from free property
and not from sold property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the two sides of the argument that רבא pointed to
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל: the late ערב pays from free property. בן ננס: he pays nothing at all.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל asks for the reason
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל asks בן ננס why the ערב should owe nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל asks בן ננס to explain his ruling. This short question sets up בן ננס's reasoning in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ערב clearly promised to pay. So רבי ישמעאל wants to know why that promise should mean nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Why?

phrases.english: He said to him: Why?
phrases.notes: רבי ישמעאל is the one asking, and he is asking בן ננס.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind בן ננס's ruling
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a late ערב's promise creates no debt at all

steps.title: בן ננס: the man in the market
steps.stepSummary: Someone stops a lender from choking a borrower by saying 'I'll pay you.' He owes nothing, because the loan was not given on his trust.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If someone was choking his friend in the market, and another friend found him and said 'Leave him alone and I will pay you,' he is exempt. The lender did not lend the money because he trusted him.
steps.whatsHappening: בן ננס explains his view with a clear example. A person who promises to pay only after the loan was already made owes nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערב owes money because the lender gave the loan trusting him. Someone who joins only after the loan was made was not part of the reason the lender gave it. So his words alone create no debt, and the late ערב is in the same position.

keyTerms.meaning: Choking, strangling
Leave him alone
Exempt, does not have to pay
His trust, his reliability

steps.whatToRemember: בן ננס's rule: a ערב owes money only if the loan was given trusting him. A promise made after the loan creates no debt.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up רבא's comparison. The question is whether words alone, without the lender relying on them, can make someone owe money. That is the same issue as the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה חוֹנֵק אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשּׁוּק,
phrases.english: He said to him: Suppose someone was choking his fellow in the marketplace,
phrases.notes: The lender is grabbing the borrower to force him to pay what he owes.

phrases.english: and a friend found him and said to him:
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is part of the corrected wording, so read it as 'found him.'

phrases.english: 'Leave him alone, and I will give you the money,'
he is exempt, because the lender did not lend the money trusting him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה חוֹנֵק אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי ישמעאל's question in Step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A promise made after the loan was given does not bind, because the lender did not rely on that person when he lent the money.

steps.title: Suggesting the two arguments match
steps.stepSummary: רבא proposes that רבי יוחנן holds like רבי ישמעאל and ריש לקיש holds like בן ננס.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say that רבי יוחנן ruled like רבי ישמעאל, and ריש לקיש ruled like בן ננס.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his comparison. He suggests that the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש is really the same as the older argument between רבי ישמעאל and בן ננס. This is a proposal, and the גמרא is about to test it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל says a person can become obligated just by taking it on himself, even though the loan was not given because of him. That fits רבי יוחנן, who says a written obligation binds. בן ננס says such a person owes nothing, which seems to fit ריש לקיש.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say: a word that introduces a suggestion the גמרא will test

phrases.english: Let us say that רבי יוחנן, who said his ruling,
phrases.notes: This is his ruling that a person who writes 'I owe you' in a document is obligated.

phrases.english: said it in line with רבי ישמעאל,
and ריש לקיש said his ruling in line with בן ננס.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the רבי ישמעאל and בן ננס case from steps 10-12 to explain the argument between the אמוראים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Suggested: רבי יוחנן follows רבי ישמעאל, and ריש לקיש follows בן ננס.

steps.title: According to בן ננס, there is no argument
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the simple matching: according to בן ננס, both רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to בן ננס, everyone agrees and nobody argues.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion. It says that if you follow בן ננס, there would be no disagreement at all. It is setting up the next line, which will show where they really argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under בן ננס's view, even רבי יוחנן would agree that a person who writes 'I owe you 100' does not have to pay. So the argument between the אמוראים cannot be the same as the argument between רבי ישמעאל and בן ננס. Their real disagreement must lie within רבי ישמעאל's view.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the view of
Everyone (here, both רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש)
They do not argue

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean everyone rules like בן ננס. It only means that if you start from בן ננס's view, the two אמוראים would agree.

phrases.english: According to the view of בן ננס,
everyone agrees and does not argue,

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּבֶן נַנָּס כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion in step 13 that the two arguments line up one-to-one.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the matching of ריש לקיש to בן ננס as the source of the argument. It does not reject the rulings themselves.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under בן ננס's view both אמוראים would agree, so their argument cannot be the same as the argument between רבי ישמעאל and בן ננס.
